Vignette: Margaret, Age 51

Margaret has worked for the same regional government office for nearly two decades, processing planning applications and coordinating between departments. She describes her job as predictable, even monotonous at times — and she has come to value that monotony deeply, in a way she never expected she would.

Three years ago, Margaret was among a group of civil servants relocated temporarily to an older government building while their main office underwent renovation. Within the first week, several employees noticed a sharp, chemical smell coming through the ventilation system. Margaret remembers dismissing it initially, assuming it was something to do with the building's age. By the second week, she was experiencing burning in her throat and eyes, persistent headaches, and a sensation she describes as "my lungs not working properly." When she raised concerns with the facilities manager, she was told the air quality had been checked and was within acceptable limits. She continued working.

It was not until a colleague collapsed at her desk and was taken by ambulance that the building was evacuated. Subsequent investigation identified a significant leak of industrial solvent from a storage room adjacent to the ventilation system. Margaret and several colleagues had been exposed for nearly ten days. She spent two nights in hospital being monitored for respiratory damage and was eventually discharged with a referral to occupational health.

Physically, she recovered. But something shifted in the weeks that followed, and it has not shifted back.

Margaret now finds herself hypervigilant in a way that exhausts her. She cannot enter a room without scanning for smells — cleaning products, paint, petrol, a neighbour's air freshener — and when she detects something unfamiliar, her body responds before her mind can intervene. Her heart rate climbs, her chest tightens, and she has to leave. She has stopped using the staff kitchen at work because the industrial cleaning solution used on the floors triggers an immediate wave of nausea and panic. Her colleagues have noticed, though most say nothing.

She sleeps poorly. Several nights a week she wakes in the early hours convinced she cannot breathe, certain that something in the air is wrong. Her husband, David, has learned to reach for her hand in the dark without being asked. She is grateful for this and ashamed of it in equal measure. She describes herself as "not someone who falls apart," and there is a quiet grief in the way she says it.

Intrusive memories surface unpredictably. She will be reviewing a planning document and suddenly find herself back at her desk in that building, throat burning, wondering whether the strange taste in the air is something she should be worried about. The memory carries with it the particular horror of not having known — of having sat there, day after day, trusting that someone would have told her if it were dangerous. That betrayal of institutional trust sits at the centre of much of her distress. She had believed in the systems she worked within. She is no longer sure she does.

She has reduced her social life considerably. She declines invitations to restaurants, newly renovated spaces, or anywhere she cannot assess in advance. She researches venues online before agreeing to go anywhere, looking for information about recent refurbishments or cleaning practices. She knows this is excessive. Knowing does not help.

At work, she is still competent and conscientious — her performance reviews remain strong — but she describes operating on a kind of controlled autopilot, keeping her attention tightly focused on the task in front of her so there is no room for her mind to wander back. She has told almost no one what she is carrying. Her manager knows she had "a health incident." That is all.

What Margaret returns to, again and again, is a simple and devastating question: Why didn't anyone listen when we said something was wrong? She does not yet have an answer that satisfies her.
